reason: Nodose cells or cell walls with knob-like thickenings are real, for example in mosses. The knobbled reading fits.
Aporose means having no pores, and leaves (for example Sphagnum) can lack pores on a surface. Imperforate fits.
Capsule margins can be ciliate, but 'endostome cilia' belong to the peristome, not the capsule. A rule would need to tell the part that carries the cilia apart from the capsule.
Globular or spherical pods are botanically meaningful, and the examples are correct.
A rudimentary staminode is a reduced, vestigial organ, so vestigial fits.
Flattened style branches are meaningful. The part is a FLOPO anatomy class with no label in the data I was given.
The examples are 'entre-nœuds' (internodes), not nodes, so this is a wrong reading. A node has almost no length. Map internode lengths to an internode part.
A cyme has a width, and the examples give it.
A sunken or immersed primary vein on the upper face is a standard leaf character.
A pistillode has dimensions. Some 'L × W' orders are ambiguous, so check that the second number is read as width.
Lengths in mm are meaningful for this anatomy class, and the examples are correct.
A loose or dense capitulum arrangement is meaningful. Some examples really describe the corymbs the capitula are grouped in.
A thickened rachis is meaningful, and the examples are correct.
Flattened disc glands and similar parts are meaningful.
The presence of an ochrea is a valid character. One example, 'veins numerous', is a wrong reading, so the item needs a check.
Sessile seed cones are meaningful, and the examples are correct.
Solitary or cespitose rosettes describe their spatial pattern.
Dark petals or dark petal tips and veins are meaningful. Some examples are about veins and midribs, which are only parts of the petal.
A dull or shining seed coat is a standard character.
Bulb dimensions are meaningful. 'Bulbs generally 2–20+' is a count, not a height, so those rows are wrong.
Samara shape (elliptic, obovate and so on) is meaningful.
'2n = 2x' states ploidy, but chromosome counts like '2n = 32' or 'n = 2' do not say diploid by themselves. A rule would need to tell ploidy statements from plain chromosome counts.
Broad involucral bracts are meaningful. One example is about bract margins, a sub-part.
A short or decreased length is meaningful for this anatomy class.
'Coarse' for a rhizome often means thick or stout, not rough. A rule would need to tell texture from stoutness.
Subulate (awl-shaped) parts are meaningful, and the examples are correct.
The lengths are those of cilia or of the leaf, not of the margin, which is a wrong-part reading. A margin is an edge and has no length of its own.
The presence of a cypsela (the fruit type) is valid.
A retuse apex is meaningful and the examples are correct.
Minute or small tubercles are meaningful.
Spike thickness in mm is meaningful and the examples are correct.
'Culms central' describes where the stem sits in the tuft, a position and not a quality of the stem. A rule would need to tell position from shape.
'Optical quality' is too generic. The examples (pale, light green) are colour, brightness or saturation, so use those terms.
Obtuse mostly describes the teeth, which are a different part, though 'margins broadly rounded' is a margin. A rule would need to tell the teeth from the margin.
Flexuous hairs are meaningful and sinuous matches.
A glandular gynoecium (ovary or style) is meaningful.
Elaiosome length in mm is meaningful.
Mucilaginous parenchyma is meaningful and mucoid fits.
Fringed tepals are meaningful.
A pale or pallid bracteole fits low saturation, though pale could also be a brightness term.
'Sparse' tells how many thorns the stem or leaf bears, not a quality of one thorn. Use a count or density on the bearing part.
The presence of glochids is a valid character.
The examples describe the umbilicus, the suture or the cupule, not the depth of the whole fruit. This is a wrong-part reading.
V-shaped bracts (in cross-section) are meaningful.
A scabrid or scabridulous bract surface is a texture character.
Winged or alate spores (perispore flange) are meaningful.
A fragile fruit or pericarp is meaningful.
A tapered petal base is meaningful.
The examples are about a persistent cortex or cork layer, a sub-part. A rule would need to tell the rhizome from its cortex.
A pentagonal stem in cross-section is meaningful.
A hispidulous involucre is meaningful and the examples are correct.
'Characteristic' is a PATO root term that is far too generic to annotate with. Use the specific quality, such as glandular or ascending.
'Scattered' describes the hairs, scales or glands on the lamina, not the lamina itself. Use the trichome or gland as bearer.
'Peduncle 1–5 mm' is a length, not a pedunculate state, while 'shortly pedunculate' is valid. A rule would need to tell lengths from the pedunculate state.
Oblong plicae or parts are meaningful.
An oblique receptacle is meaningful, as in Asteraceae.
An immersed or sunken columella is meaningful for mosses.
A slender perianth tube or base is meaningful.
The examples are about the midrib or veins being unbranched, not the lamina. This is a wrong-part reading, so use the vein or midrib as bearer.
The examples are about the cortex, hyalodermis or nodules not being differentiated, which are sub-parts. This is a wrong-part reading, so use the cortex as bearer.
